claims.text: The nanoparticles are initially solid, single-phase FCC FeNiCrCoCu particles.
The nanoparticles have diameters of 5–10 nm.
The nanoparticles have uniform bulk composition at room temperature.
Preferential segregation of Cu to the nanoparticle surface governs the onset and progression of premelting and melting.
Surface-segregated Cu forms a lower-melting, liquid-like nanoshell.
The liquid-like nanoshell nucleates at the surface at approximately 0.8 times the bulk melting temperature.
The liquid-like shell thickens inward as temperature increases.
The bulk melting temperature of FeNiCrCoCu is approximately 1600 K.
Heating causes Cu atoms to diffuse and segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Cu enrichment locally lowers the melting point of the nanoparticle surface.
A disordered, mobile surface layer forms at approximately 0.8 times the bulk melting temperature.
Growth of the liquid-like surface layer eventually causes complete melting of the particle core.
At approximately 0.8 times the bulk melting temperature, the Cu-containing nanoparticles will exhibit a disordered, Cu-rich shell about 1–2 atomic layers thick.
At approximately 0.9 times the bulk melting temperature, the Cu-rich shell will be about 1–2 nm thick.
Cu-containing nanoparticles will show a DSC melting onset approximately 100 K below the bulk melting temperature.
Cu-free FeNiCrCo nanoparticles will melt closer to their bulk melting temperature than Cu-containing nanoparticles.
Cu-free FeNiCrCo nanoparticles will not exhibit observable premelting.
The proposed behavior applies to 5–10 nm nanoparticles heated at no more than 10 K/min in an inert atmosphere.

contradictions.description: With the stated bulk melting temperature of about 1600 K, 0.8 T_m is about 1280 K, or roughly 320 K below T_m. This conflicts with or at least leaves unresolved the separate prediction that DSC melting onset occurs only about 100 K below T_m. The text does not explain whether these are intentionally different definitions or detection thresholds for surface premelting versus calorimetric melting onset.
